Any alternate publishing credentials or bypass path would undermine fail-closed enforcement.

artifact.simplest_viable_option: Create one required GitHub Actions release workflow that blocks publishing unless the version differs from the last release, the changelog contains that version, migration changes receive designated approval, and smoke tests pass. Restrict publishing credentials to this workflow.
artifact.change_my_mind_evidence: Adopt semantic-release or changesets sooner if releases occur more than weekly, version or changelog mistakes remain common despite gates, commit history is already reliably conventional, or independent package versions are causing release errors. Consider a thin CLI only if essential release operations must occur outside CI.
artifact.next_step: Define the monorepo versioning model, migration-change trigger, exact smoke command, and canonical release artifact; then implement and require the single GitHub Actions release workflow.

artifact.recommendation: Adopt a narrow release-PR bot enforced by GitHub Actions: use release-please for unified versioning or Changesets for independently versioned packages; automate version bumps, changelog generation, and smoke-runs; require migration approval through a protected GitHub Environment. Keep publishing credentials exclusively in CI. Do not build a custom CLI or rely on PR-template checkboxes.
artifact.confidence: High (89%). Architect and Pragmatist independently converge on CI-enforced automation; the Skeptic timed out, so no adversarial assessment was available. Exact bot choice remains uncertain until the monorepo versioning model is known.
artifact.consensus: The successful panelists agree that GitHub Actions must be the enforcement boundary, a release PR should provide an inspectable checkpoint, mechanical work should be automated, migration judgment should remain a blocking human gate, and neither a custom CLI nor PR-template checkboxes meets the goal of requiring less discipline.
disagreements: The Architect recommends a semantic-release-style workflow generically; the Pragmatist specifically prefers release-please and argues semantic-release imposes conventional-commit and monorepo complexity.
Effort estimates differ: Architect estimates 2–4 engineering days, while Pragmatist estimates roughly half a day plus one or two releases of stabilization.
The Pragmatist suggests initially using a general Environment reviewer gate for migrations; the Architect more explicitly calls for migration detection and migration-owner approval.
strongest_evidence: Architect: A custom CLI still depends on someone running it and creates maintenance overhead for only three releasers.
Architect: A PR checklist records claims but proves nothing, adding discipline rather than removing it.
Pragmatist: If publishing is wired exclusively through GitHub Actions, failed smoke jobs and required Environment approvals become actual release blockers.
Pragmatist: release-please generates an inspectable release PR without requiring the conventional-commit discipline associated with semantic-release.
Pragmatist: The monorepo versioning model is decisive—release-please fits coupled versions, while Changesets fits independently versioned packages.
Architect: Human approval should remain only where judgment is genuinely required, namely migration review.
assumptions: Production publishing or deployment can run from GitHub Actions.
Smoke checks can be automated at least enough to produce a blocking pass or fail result.
Migration-bearing changes can be detected from paths, labels, or another deterministic repository signal.
Release PR metadata is sufficiently structured to derive versions and changelog entries.
GitHub Environment protection is available for the repository and plan.
risks: Choosing the wrong versioning model could produce incorrect package releases.
Poor PR labels or commit metadata could create incorrect bumps or changelog entries.
A broad Environment approval may become a rubber stamp unless migration detection targets the correct reviewer.
Manual publishing credentials left on developer machines would permit bypassing every CI gate.
Smoke automation may create false confidence if it does not exercise the critical release path.
Bot and action dependencies require pinning and occasional maintenance.
blind_spots: The Skeptic panelist failed, leaving no dedicated adversarial critique.
Release frequency and cost of prior misses were not provided.
It is unknown whether packages use unified or independent versions.
Current smoke-test availability, deployment target, migration layout, and rollback behavior are unspecified.
Repository permissions and GitHub plan support for required Environment reviewers are unknown.
artifact.simplest_viable_option: Add one release-PR bot workflow, one blocking smoke job, and one protected production Environment approval. Use release-please if versions move together; use Changesets if packages version independently. Defer custom dashboards, CLI frameworks, fully unattended publishing, and sophisticated migration automation.
artifact.change_my_mind_evidence: Prefer a tiny local release script only if publishing cannot safely run in GitHub Actions due to signing, air-gap, or platform constraints. Consider a custom CLI only after measured workflow limitations prove existing bots cannot express required release logic. A checklist alone becomes reasonable only for rare, low-impact releases where automation cost clearly exceeds repeated failure cost.
artifact.next_step: Determine whether package versions are unified or independent, then prototype the matching bot in dry-run/release-PR mode and define deterministic migration detection plus the minimum smoke command required to block publishing.
